### 164-29 — Scan 176; `MPL_147_138-190_scan176.tex`, lines 2–5 and 19, (292) — unproved claim — The heuristic homeomorphism needs a neighborhood comparison theorem

The correction to “‘homéomorphie’ (heuristique !)” explicitly stops short of a constructed equivalence between the normal-bundle model and the neighborhood topos. This **adds** a nonlinear neighborhood comparison to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 122 and 127, which construct normal line bundles and induced normal-crossing strata but do not identify their neighborhoods with their normal bundles. A proof would need a topological tubular model preserving the relevant partial boundary deletions, followed by a comparison with the chosen topos or germ construction. The existence of a normal bundle by itself establishes neither a holomorphic linearization nor a canonical homeomorphism, and neither stronger conclusion should be read into (292).

“Sauf erreur, on peut” announces a globalization into strata with intrinsic topologies and a bijective local immersion $D^*_{\Delta_0}\to X$. This **adds** a construction from local equivalence data to the local immersions already built from analytic branch germs in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 107–108, and to the globally immersed examples in scan 121. One must construct the equivalence relation generated by local pieces, prove independence of representatives and compatibility of the intrinsic topologies, and distinguish a bijective local immersion from a homeomorphism onto $X$. The SGA exercise is an explicit source lead, not a proof until its hypotheses and conclusions are matched to these particular local strata.

“Si $X$ est compact” is used to obtain finitely many intrinsic strata, “qui sont loc. compactes,” with the warning that finiteness need not survive restriction to an open set. This **adds** a global finiteness conclusion to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 106–108, where finiteness concerns branch sets at individual points, not the number of global strata. A proof can try a finite cover by charts with finitely many local pieces, but must justify that each local connected piece belongs to one globally constructed stratum; local compactness additionally requires the relevant separation convention and locally closed chart models. These are separate checks, and neither follows simply from finiteness of the local incidence posets.

The claimed homeomorphism (298) says that the new notation “coïncide” with the earlier normal-crossing construction. This **restates** the coproduct and first-vertex restriction in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 129, equation (206), while **adding** the interpretation as global intrinsic strata obtained from local stratification data. The proof should match individual local branches and their monodromy identifications, including self-intersection phenomena, rather than treating a codimension label as sufficient to identify the deployed spaces.

The extension to “une immersion locale de topos” is qualified by “sauf erreur,” so the general topos construction is not established here. It adds a new neighborhood operation to the site-independent flag axioms of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 118–119, and to the tentative topos interpretation of germ coverings in `LM_140-4_text.tex`, scans 242–243. One must define the intended class of immersions and the relevant limit of localizations, then prove that composition supplies the indicated morphism of germs; the existence of slice topoi alone does not settle that neighborhood problem (Artin et al., 1972, Exposé IV, §5).

“‘Normalisé topologique’ … dans un sens à préciser” leaves the construction of $D_d$ open after the shift away from fundamental groupoids. This restates geometrically the branch-germ space defined in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 107–108, and differs from the purely site-theoretic flag axioms on scans 114–119. The point to settle is what replaces analytic normalization in the purely topological normal-crossing setting: separating local branches is a candidate operation, but its topology, local immersion property, and behavior under monodromy require an explicit construction.

The combination of “topos quasi-galoisien” with a topological category of strata suggests comparing the proposed reconstruction with a stratified shape rather than immediately taking an ordinary groupoid. This **adds** a potential bridge to the noninvertible specialization data of `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 163–166, and the site-independent flag axioms in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 118: Barwick et al. (2020, §§0.4.7 and 0.5.2, in the author PDF checked here) classify suitable constructible sheaves of $\pi$-finite spaces using profinite stratified shapes, with a Galois-category description for quasicompact quasiseparated schemes. Confidence is medium in this as a useful comparison problem because both constructions retain specialization, but the manuscript's analytic germ flags are not thereby identified with the profinite category of geometric points and étale specializations. Establishing a comparison would require an actual functor, precise coefficients and continuity, and the relevant stratified-topos hypotheses; neither the general analytic case nor full homotopy recovery follows automatically from that theorem.
### 190-01 — The Boolean condition fails independently of the category axioms

The three-ray drawing has seven incident strata “en comptant $\bullet$ lui-$=$,” so its local order cannot be the full powerset of a finite set. This **differs** from the normal-crossing hypothesis in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 106 and 116, and **adds** an explicit witness that the general local-stratification framework has non-Boolean incidence. The count is interpreted in the planar model as the centre, three rays, and three sectors; it does not by itself disprove the Segal identity, finite étaleness, or any particular homotopy-reconstruction assertion. A useful axiomatization should therefore keep the Boolean local-order condition separate from the categorical and topological conditions.

Use “on n'a pas fait usage” as a proof-organizing test: first establish the germ-incidence category from the local partition axioms, then mark exactly where stronger neighbourhood hypotheses are required for homotopy comparisons. This **adds** a way to audit the separation already made in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 132–133, between formal flag-cover relations and nonformal generisation, and prevents the success of the former from being treated as a proof of the latter. Confidence is medium-high because both manuscripts explicitly draw this distinction, while the detailed implication diagram among a)–e), finite source covers, tubular fibrations, and homotopy descent still has to be proved. The sphere and the non-Boolean planar example provide complementary tests of that separation.

The phrase “de noyau un quotient de $T_{d_0,\ldots,d_r}$” is consistent with the exact sequence $\pi_2(B)\to\pi_1((\mathbb C^*)^r)\to\pi_1(P)\to\pi_1(B)\to1$ for a locally trivial torus bundle over a connected base. It qualifies the extension description in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 130–131, where the margin already warns that the full lattice kernel requires a condition on $\pi_2$. The connecting homomorphism can kill meridians, so a proof should identify its image and the induced local-system action rather than assert an injection of the entire lattice; the fibration exact sequence is the relevant classical result (Serre, 1949–1950, §1).

A useful test of “un quotient de $T$” and “par l’image des $\pi_2$” is the zero-section divisor in the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$: its punctured normal bundle identifies with $\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\}$ by sending a nonzero vector in its tautological line to that vector. This total space retracts to $S^3$, so its fundamental group is zero, whereas the trivial punctured line bundle over $\mathbb P^1$ has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$; the contrast is the Hopf-bundle instance of the connecting map discussed by Serre (1949–1950, §§1, 5). This **adds** an explicit example to the normal-line torsors of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 122–123, and the $\pi_2$ caveat on scan 130, and tests the models on current scans 175–178 as well as the earlier qualification on scan 148. Confidence is high in the calculation because the identification is explicit, and medium in its usefulness for the full diagram comparison because one piece does not settle canonical transition maps; no claim is made that this particular bundle occurs in the moduli application.

The canceled, unfinished “Supposons que … $D_i^{*\infty}\leftrightarrow1$” begins a condition on the boundary structures and then selects an open-and-closed submultiplicity $D'_i$, but never supplies a conclusion. It **adds** an abandoned possible simplification to the punctured-torsor framework in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 123 and 130, where nontrivial torus fibers and the possible contribution of $\pi_2$ already obstruct an indiscriminate replacement of the data by points. The exact intended strength of the displayed relation with $1$, the scope of the index condition, and the role of the partially legible insertion remain reading questions; this is not a surviving corollary about contractibility. The later $K(\pi,1)$ expectation and its correction on scans 179–180 concern a different, explicitly discussed hypothesis and do not complete the deleted sentence.

The remark that normal crossings “ne joue plus de rôle depuis belle lurette” needs a specified scope when $X$ is replaced by a possibly singular admissible $\Sigma''$. It **differs** from `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 126 and 133, which expressly assign a nonformal role to normal-crossing neighborhood geometry in constructing the complete generization system. Current scans 189–190 later isolate global finite étaleness, manifold strata, and Boolean branch incidence as special properties, while reserving local triviality for tubular constructions. Read as a statement about the formal incidence category, the remark has a narrower plausible meaning; read as preserving every geometric property of the earlier construction under restriction, it remains unsupported by the passages cited.

The admission that the reduction “ne s’explicite pas aisément, au niveau des groupoïdes fondamentaux” concerns information lost when passing from a closed immersion of topoi to its induced groupoid map. It **restates** the distinction between the mixed recollement topos and its multigaloisian reflection in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scans 163–166, and **adds** the concrete problem of recovering open complements from that reduced data. A simple illustration is that both pairs $(\mathbb C,\{0\})$ and $(\mathbb C,\mathbb C)$ induce, up to equivalence, the same arrow of trivial connected fundamental groupoids, while their open complements have respectively fundamental group $\mathbb Z$ and no objects. This illustration concerns the bare groupoid arrow, and scan 180 supplies a separate warning about higher cohomology lost by a proposed constructible reconstruction; neither warning identifies the comparison in `LM_140-2_text.tex`, scan 167, with the one refuted on 180.

The statement “peut se décrire comme un produit fibré” proposes the defining square for the partially punctured neighborhood topos. This **adds** a nonformal neighborhood operation to `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 132–133, which carefully separates finite-cover base changes from the additional structure requiring normal crossings. A proof needs a site or germ construction for both neighborhood objects, a well-defined map induced by $A\subset B$, and a base-change theorem identifying the pullback with partial puncturing. Checking the square in a polydisc is necessary, but it does not by itself establish the global equivalence of topoi.

The inserted phrase “fibré conormal” accompanies an exact sequence with the usual direction of a normal-bundle sequence. This **differs** from the explicit “faisceau normal” construction in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 122, while `LM_140-3_text.tex`, scan 293, shows that a check accent can also occur in the geometric-vector-bundle notation $\check V(\mathcal N)$. Under the standard convention for $Z\hookrightarrow Y\hookrightarrow X$, the conormal sequence starts with $\mathcal C_{Y/X}|_Z$, and dualizing a locally split exact sequence gives $0\to N_{Z/Y}\to N_{Z/X}\to N_{Y/X}|_Z\to0$ (Stacks Project Authors, 2026a, §37.63(4); 2026c, Lemma 31.22.6). This is a convention/readability question for the displayed symbols, not authorization to replace “conormal,” reverse arrows, or remove an accent in the transcription.

The instruction “en prenant le produit des fibrés principaux associés” makes $N^*$ the locus where every line-factor coordinate is nonzero. It **restates** the product of punctured normal lines in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scan 122, and extends the single-line equivalence between a punctured line bundle and a $G_m$-torsor noted in `LM_140-3_text.tex`, scan 350. For rank greater than one this differs from the complement of only the zero section, so the divisor-induced line factors and their permutation transitions are essential additional structure. Deligne (1989, §15.1) gives a published comparison for a normal-crossing divisor by defining the complement of all coordinate hyperplane subbundles, but this definition alone does not prove the manuscript’s subsequent neighborhood equivalence.

The assertion “est un torseur sous le fibré vectoriel” follows formally if (287), after its notation is settled, is a short exact sequence $0\to K\to E\xrightarrow{q}Q\to0$ of vector bundles and the indicated open subset is $Q^*\subset Q$. It **adds** a higher-rank instance of the affine-bundle/translation-bundle relation in `LM_140-3_text.tex`, scans 294, 296, and 299. Translation by the pulled-back kernel acts on $q^{-1}(Q^*)$, two lifts of the same point differ by exactly one element of that kernel, and local splittings of the sequence supply local sections. This proves the torsor claim under the stated hypotheses while leaving open the correct manuscript indices and any claim of a canonical section.

The emphatic “est une équivalence d’homotopie” concerns the projection of the affine torsor onto the punctured quotient bundle. It **adds** a topological conclusion to the affine-translation distinction in `LM_140-3_text.tex`, scans 294 and 299. For an actual locally trivial affine bundle over a paracompact analytic-manifold base, a partition of unity combines local affine sections into a continuous section, and affine interpolation contracts each fiber toward it, giving a direct proof without requiring a holomorphic splitting. The remaining obligation is to identify the manuscript objects with such bundles before transporting this argument to a germ or topos model.

The phrase “de noyau un quotient de $T_{d_0,\ldots,d_r}$” is consistent with the exact sequence $\pi_2(B)\to\pi_1((\mathbb C^*)^r)\to\pi_1(P)\to\pi_1(B)\to1$ for a locally trivial torus bundle over a connected base. It qualifies the extension description in `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 130–131, where the margin already warns that the full lattice kernel requires a condition on $\pi_2$. The connecting homomorphism can kill meridians, so a proof should identify its image and the induced local-system action rather than assert an injection of the entire lattice; the fibration exact sequence is the relevant classical result (Serre, 1949–1950, §1).

A useful test of “un quotient de $T$” and “par l’image des $\pi_2$” is the zero-section divisor in the total space of $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$: its punctured normal bundle identifies with $\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\}$ by sending a nonzero vector in its tautological line to that vector. This total space retracts to $S^3$, so its fundamental group is zero, whereas the trivial punctured line bundle over $\mathbb P^1$ has fundamental group $\mathbb Z$; the contrast is the Hopf-bundle instance of the connecting map discussed by Serre (1949–1950, §§1, 5). This **adds** an explicit example to the normal-line torsors of `ARCH_147_003-137_text.tex`, scans 122–123, and the $\pi_2$ caveat on scan 130, and tests the models on current scans 175–178 as well as the earlier qualification on scan 148.
